title: The rise of the UK warehouse and the “golden logistics triangle”
meta_description: The growth in online shopping has contributed to an increase in the number of warehouses and other logistics premises in the UK, with the so-called “golden logistics triangle” of the Midlands having expanded.

breadcrumb.text: The rise of the UK warehouse and the “golden logistics triangle”

lede: The growth in online shopping has contributed to an increase in the number of warehouses and other logistics premises in the UK, with the so-called “golden logistics triangle” of the Midlands having expanded.

body.text: 11 April 2022
The number of business premises used for transport, logistics and warehousing in the UK has almost doubled in the last decade, new analysis shows.

As well as the Midlands, home to the “golden logistics triangle”, these premises are now most concentrated in parts of the East of England and Yorkshire and The Humber that were not previously associated with the industry.

body.box_text:
The “golden logistics triangle”

The phrase “golden logistics triangle” is believed to have originated in the late 1980s and covered an area around Magna Park in Lutterworth. It was so called because of its connectivity with the rest of the country.

We have estimated a “golden logistics triangle” that is within a four-hour drive of 90% of the British population. The area covers 289 square miles in the West Midlands, which is around half the size of London.

More details about the method and its limitations are available in [Measuring the data](#data).

body.text: The rise of transport and storage has accelerated in the last two years, following EU exit and the onset of the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic.

[Online shopping as a percentage of retail sales](https://www.ons.gov.uk/businessindustryandtrade/retailindustry/timeseries/j4mc/drsi), [new orders for the building of warehouses](https://www.ons.gov.uk/businessindustryandtrade/constructionindustry/datasets/newordersintheconstructionindustry), and [job adverts in transport, logistics and warehousing](https://www.ons.gov.uk/economy/economicoutputandproductivity/output/bulletins/economicactivityandsocialchangeintheukrealtimeindicators/7april2022#business-and-workforce) have all increased substantially compared with before the coronavirus pandemic. This could partly reflect changes initiated by coronavirus restrictions or [supply chain adjustments made after EU exit](https://www.ons.gov.uk/businessindustryandtrade/internationaltrade/articles/earlyinsightsintotheimpactsofthecoronaviruspandemicandeuexitonbusinesssupplychainsintheuk/february2021tofebruary2022).
In 2021, the number of UK business premises classified as transport and storage was 88% higher than in 2011 and 21% higher than in 2019.
The rise since 2019 is especially notable given the overall trend – the number of business units across all industries increased by just 1% over the same period.

Business premises refer to local units on the Inter-Departmental Business Register (IDBR), which are individual sites that belong to an enterprise. Only a small minority of businesses operate more than one site (1.5% in transport and storage and 2.1% across all industries).
Transport and storage consists of passenger transport, haulage, warehousing, and postal and courier activities.

body.h2: Distribution services have driven growth of transport and storage
body.text: Distribution services have driven growth of transport and storage

body.h2: Distribution services have driven growth of transport and storage
body.text: Transport and storage remains a relatively small industry across the UK, accounting for 5% of business premises (155,000 out of 3.2 million).

body.h2: Distribution services have driven growth of transport and storage
body.text: However, it is now the largest industry in parts of the Midlands, the East of England and Yorkshire and The Humber, in terms of share of business units.

body.h2: Distribution services have driven growth of transport and storage
body.text: Growth of transport and storage in the last decade has been led by hauliers and couriers. The number of business premises classified as “freight transport by road” and “postal and courier activities” increased by 114% and 147%, respectively, between 2011 and 2021. Together, they now account for 69% of all transport and storage business units, up from 58% in 2011.

body.h2: The shift to online retail has increased demand for warehousing
body.text: The impact of the coronavirus pandemic has led to people buying online a lot more than they used to.

body.h2: The shift to online retail has increased demand for warehousing
body.text: Online shopping as a percentage of all retail sales peaked at nearly 38% in January 2021, having stood at 8% at the start of 2011 and 19% in February 2020. It has since fallen back but remains around 28% in the latest period (February 2022).

body.h2: The shift to online retail has increased demand for warehousing
body.text: This has contributed to a sharp rise in new warehouse construction projects.

body.h2: The shift to online retail has increased demand for warehousing
body.text: New orders for the building of warehouses were worth £5.6 billion in 2021; this is more than in any year since 1985.

body.h2: The shift to online retail has increased demand for warehousing
body.text: The East Midlands accounted for one-fifth (20%) of the spending in 2021, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS) new orders data supplier Barbour ABI. The other main locations for warehouse spending were Yorkshire and The Humber (16%), the East of England (13%), and the West Midlands (13%).

body.text: While the number of business premises has almost doubled in the last 10 years, employment in transport and storage was only 20% higher in December 2021 compared with the same month in 2011.

body.h2: The rate of growth in new businesses has been faster than the rate of job creation in transport and storage
body.text: This is according to our [workforce jobs by industry dataset](https://www.ons.gov.uk/employmentandlabourmarket/peopleinwork/employmentandemployeetypes/datasets/workforcejobsbyindustryjobs02), which includes employee and self-employment jobs.

body.h2: The rate of growth in new businesses has been faster than the rate of job creation in transport and storage
body.text: The difference in growth rates could reflect an increased number of small businesses, recent worker shortages, or the [potential automation of some occupations](https://www.ons.gov.uk/employmentandlabourmarket/peopleinwork/employmentandemployeetypes/articles/whichoccupationsareathighestriskofbeingautomated/2019-03-25).

body.text: The percentage of transport and storage premises with fewer than five employees increased from 67% in 2011 to 79% in 2021.

body.h2: Transport and storage workers are lower paid than average, and they work longer hours
body.text: Transport and storage workers are lower paid than average, and they work longer hours

body.h2: Transport and storage workers are lower paid than average, and they work longer hours
body.text: Hourly earnings in transport and storage were below the national average in 2021 (£14.76 compared with £15.65).

body.h2: Transport and storage workers are lower paid than average, and they work longer hours
body.text: However, only 7% of transport and storage workers were considered low paid (earning below £9.40 per hour), compared with an all-industry rate of 14%.

body.h2: Transport and storage workers are lower paid than average, and they work longer hours
body.text: Full-time staff in the transport and storage industry, such as couriers, HGV drivers and warehouse workers, worked nearly 42 hours in a typical week. The average across all industries is nearly 39 hours.

body.h2: Transport and storage workers are lower paid than average, and they work longer hours
body.text: Transport and storage workers were more likely than those in any other industry to do overtime (32%), with those working overtime recording nearly eight additional hours per week on average.

body.h2: Transport and storage workers are lower paid than average, and they work longer hours
body.text: Regional differences in pay were greater for transport and storage than on average across all industries.

body.h2: Transport and storage workers are lower paid than average, and they work longer hours
body.text: Transport and storage workers in the highest paid region (London) earned £20.12 per hour on average in 2021, compared with £12.76 in the lowest paid (the North East).

body.h2: Transport and storage workers are lower paid than average, and they work longer hours
body.text: Across all industries, average hourly earnings were £20.39 in London, compared with £13.95 in the lowest paid region (the East Midlands).

body.h2: Transport and storage workers are lower paid than average, and they work longer hours
body.text: London has the highest percentage of employment in air transport (the highest paid of the transport and storage sub-industries) of any English region.

body.h2: Transport and storage is growing fastest in parts of the Midlands, the East of England and Yorkshire and The Humber
body.text: Transport and storage business premises are increasingly concentrated in the middle of the country, in an area we have estimated as the "golden logistics triangle" and further afield.

body.h2: Transport and storage is growing fastest in parts of the Midlands, the East of England and Yorkshire and The Humber
body.text: In 2021, there were 11 local authority districts in the UK where transport and storage was the dominant industry. These included Rugby in Warwickshire, South Holland in Lincolnshire, Peterborough, and Doncaster.

body.h2: Transport and storage is growing fastest in parts of the Midlands, the East of England and Yorkshire and The Humber
body.text: By comparison, in 2011, transport and storage was not the main industry in any part of the UK.

body.h2: Transport and storage is growing fastest in parts of the Midlands, the East of England and Yorkshire and The Humber
body.text: Rugby had the highest percentage of business units used for transport and storage in the UK in 2021 (17%). Newport (10%), North Lanarkshire (8%) and Antrim and Newtownabbey (8%) were the highest ranking areas in Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland, respectively.

body.h2: Transport and storage is growing fastest in parts of the Midlands, the East of England and Yorkshire and The Humber
body.text: In terms of scale, West Northamptonshire had the highest number of business premises occupied by transport and storage (3,200), followed by Leeds (3,100), North Northamptonshire (2,700) and Birmingham (2,500).

body.text: Measuring the data

body.h2: Measuring the data
body.text: Calculating the “golden logistics triangle”

body.h2: Measuring the data
body.text: Great Britain was divided into one kilometre grid squares and Census 2011 population figures were assigned to each square.

body.h2: Measuring the data
body.text: Travel times were calculated using the Open Source Routing Machine (OSRM). This calculates times according to the travel network, not “as the crow flies”.

body.h2: Measuring the data
body.text: Using the OSRM package in R (a statistical programming language), four-hour drive time polygons were created from the centroids of each 1km grid square. The square was considered part of the “golden logistics triangle” if its polygon covered 90% or more of the British population.

body.h2: Measuring the data
body.text: This method used publicly available data and tools to estimate population and travel time. It has several limitations:

body.h2: Measuring the data
body.text: the travel time calculation does not account for traffic conditions or time of day, so it is not necessarily representative of real-world journey times

body.h2: Measuring the data
body.text: we used the "car" drive-time mode on OSRM, which may not represent the speed of slow-moving vehicles such as HGVs

body.h2: Measuring the data
body.text: additional travel time on private land that hosts a warehouse, for example, may not be accounted for; the mapping detail depends on [volunteers adding features onto OpenStreetMap](https://osmuk.org/getting-started/using-openstreetmap-map-data/)

body.h2: Measuring the data
body.text: the analysis excludes 1km squares that are uninhabited; this could mean that some warehousing areas are excluded

body.h2: Measuring the data
body.text: population changes between 2011 and 2022 have not been accounted for and the impact of these on the analysis is unknown.

body.h2: Measuring the data
body.text: The [full method and code are available on GitHub](https://github.com/ONSvisual/golden_triangle).

body.h2: Measuring the data
body.text: Business premises

body.h2: Measuring the data
body.text: Most of the analysis in this article refers to numbers of business premises, which are counts of local business units taken from the Inter-Departmental Business Register (IDBR). Local units are individual sites that belong to an enterprise.

body.h2: Measuring the data
body.text: At an enterprise level, companies are classified according to their main activity. Local units (with employees) are classified according to the main activity at that site. For example, a warehouse owned by a retail enterprise should be classified as transport and storage, because warehousing is the main activity at that particular local unit.

body.h2: Measuring the data
body.text: The IDBR is available to query on [Nomis](https://www.nomisweb.co.uk/home/release_group.asp?g=20), a data explorer tool.

body.h2: Measuring the data
body.text: New warehouse building

body.h2: Measuring the data
body.text: New orders for the construction of warehouses are published as part of [our bulletin on construction output in Great Britain](https://www.ons.gov.uk/businessindustryandtrade/constructionindustry/bulletins/constructionoutputingreatbritain/february2022).

body.h2: Measuring the data
body.text: The regional and local authority breakdowns are based on data for individual projects and provided by the new orders data supplier Barbour ABI.

body.text: Earnings and working hours

body.h2: Measuring the data
body.text: Data on earnings and working hours are taken from the Annual Survey of Hours and Earnings (ASHE).

body.h2: Measuring the data
body.text: The [2021 ASHE release](https://www.ons.gov.uk/employmentandlabourmarket/peopleinwork/earningsandworkinghours/bulletins/annualsurveyofhoursandearnings/2021/relateddata) contains breakdowns by industry and occupation.

body.h2: Measuring the data
body.text: Employment

body.h2: Measuring the data
body.text: The Business Register of Employment Survey (BRES) is the official source of employment statistics by detailed geography and industry.

body.h2: Measuring the data
body.text: Our [latest BRES release](https://www.ons.gov.uk/employmentandlabourmarket/peopleinwork/employmentandemployeetypes/bulletins/businessregisterandemploymentsurveybresprovisionalresults/provisionalresults2020) covers 2020 and can be queried on [Nomis](https://www.nomisweb.co.uk/datasets/newbres6pub).
